title: The Undemocratic School Primer
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene sketches the underlying fault line in American education debates: one side premises that all humans have equal worth and schools should uplift every child; the other premises that some are destined to be Betters and others Lessers, with schools sorting children into proper tiers. These are not two sides of a shared conversation but two conversations with shared vocabulary. Both sides can say every child deserves education best suited to them while meaning nearly opposite things. Greene reads tiered school-choice systems, narrowing of education for working-class children, and emphasis on compliance as surface expressions of the Betterist premise. He acknowledges not all choice supporters are conscious Betterists but notes there is no bridge to the position that some children are worth less. His diagnostic: if policy conversations feel like running past each other, both sides are working from fundamentally different premises about what children are for and what democracy owes them. Naming the premise is the first step in honest disagreement.
points: The underlying fault line in education debates is not about policies but about whether all children have equal worth or some are destined for lower tiers.
Both sides can say 'every child deserves education best suited to them' while meaning nearly opposite things; they speak a shared vocabulary but have fundamentally different premises.
Policy moves like tiered school choice, narrowed curricula for working-class children, and emphasis on compliance are surface expressions of the Betterist premise, not stand-alone disputes.
quotes: There are many ways to divide up the sides of the education debates. One is between those who believe in civic democratic ideals and those who do not.

Premise 1: All human beings have equal worth and are equally deserving of autonomy, opportunity, power, and privilege. Under this premise, the school system would exist to provide opportunity to all students.

Premise 2: Some human beings have more value than others, and are more deserving of autonomy, power, and privilege. In that world, schools exist not for uplift, but for sorting, to help everyone find and settle happily into their proper place.

Betters may learn arts and culture and what we think of as a broad liberal education. But future meat widgets need to learn marketable skills, job skills that will make them useful to their future corporate-boss Betters.

For Lessers, obedience and compliance are important. Schools are supposed to reinforce that message, reminding students that they are under the sole and complete control of their parents and must never, ever question that control.

It’s not always easy to talk through the issues with them because some of the words have different meanings; we can all say that every child should get the education they deserve or that is best suited to them, but we mean different things.
Nor are all school choice fans bettersists. I’m not even sure that some school choice fans really understand who they’ve teamed up with.

Betterists pose a real challenge to any sort of discussion or debate about education in this country, because they hold a fundamentally different view of the purpose of education, a profoundly different idea about how the country is supposed to work.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
